stories.original:
**Seventeen banks to pilot live transactions on Swift's shared ledger**

*Swift is moving its blockchain-based interoperable ledger from sandbox to live transactions, with seventeen banks across six countries testing tokenised deposits for round-the-clock settlement.*

The pilot marks a meaningful escalation from Swift's earlier proof-of-concept work on distributed ledger technology. By using tokenised deposits rather than a new settlement asset, Swift is testing whether existing correspondent banking relationships can support 24/7 payment availability and more efficient liquidity management without requiring participants to adopt an entirely new infrastructure.

Seventeen banks from six countries will participate, though Swift has not disclosed which institutions or jurisdictions are involved. The focus on interoperability — connecting tokenised deposits across different ledger implementations — addresses a practical weakness that has limited earlier DLT settlement experiments, where isolated platforms struggled to achieve the network effects needed for real-world adoption.

The move comes as central banks and market infrastructures are reaching divergent conclusions about DLT's readiness for wholesale settlement. The Bank of England flagged "significant trade-offs" in its own assessment last May. Swift's approach sidesteps some of those concerns by layering tokenisation onto existing messaging infrastructure rather than replacing settlement systems wholesale.

*Sources: [Banks to pilot live transactions on Swift's blockchain-based shared ledger](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48060/banks-to-pilot-live-transactions-on-swifts-blockchain-based-shared-ledger) — Finextra*

**Montenegro adopts instant payments law to align with EU SEPA standards**

*Montenegro has passed legislation enabling instant payments based on SEPA standards, with a launch date of July 20, extending the EU's instant payments infrastructure into the Western Balkans.*

The law clears the path for Montenegro to go live with instant payments on July 20, using infrastructure provided by the Bank of Italy, which operates TIPS-based services for central banks outside the eurozone. Montenegro joins a growing list of non-EU countries connecting to European instant payment rails, following Iceland's recent TIPS connection.

For Montenegro, the move is both a practical modernisation step and a signal of EU alignment ahead of its accession process. The country's adoption of SEPA standards rather than a purely domestic system means its banks will be interoperable with eurozone counterparts from launch, reducing the friction that typically accompanies cross-border retail payments in candidate countries.

The pattern of SEPA-standard adoption spreading beyond the eurozone's formal borders reinforces the EU instant payments regulation's gravitational pull. Each new connection extends the network's reach and strengthens the case for SEPA instant as the default European retail payment rail.

*Sources: [Adoption of law a condition for instant payments](https://en.vijesti.me/news-b/economy-d/816915/adoption-of-the-law-is-a-condition-for-instant-payments) — Vijesti | [Montenegro to launch instant payments on July 20 using SEPA standards](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48060/) — previously covered item*

stories.original:
**Scottish Power uses open banking data for energy affordability checks**

*Scottish Power has partnered with AperiData to offer customers digital affordability assessments using open banking data, extending open finance use cases beyond financial services into utilities.*

The service lets Scottish Power customers share bank transaction data to demonstrate affordability or access support, replacing manual income verification with real-time open banking connections. AperiData, which PayPoint acquired in June, provides the underlying data aggregation and affordability scoring.

Energy is a natural adjacent sector for open banking affordability tools. Utilities face many of the same challenges as lenders — assessing ability to pay, identifying customers in financial difficulty, managing arrears — but have historically lacked access to the transaction-level data that financial services firms use. The FCA's open finance roadmap and the UK's broader smart data programme have both pointed toward exactly this kind of cross-sector data sharing.

The partnership illustrates how open banking infrastructure built for payments and lending is finding commercial traction in regulated sectors where affordability assessment is either required or commercially valuable. It also validates PayPoint's rationale for acquiring AperiData: building open banking into credit and affordability data services beyond traditional financial services.

*Sources: [Scottish Power teams up with AperiData to introduce digital affordability service](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/scottish-power-teams-up-with-aperidata-to-introduce-digital-affordability-service/) — Open Banking Expo*

stories.original:
**French Banking Federation frames payment sovereignty as strategic priority**

*The French Banking Federation has published a position paper arguing that European payment sovereignty requires coordinated support for Wero, instant payments and domestic infrastructure to reduce dependence on non-European networks.*

The paper sets out French banks' view that payment sovereignty is not merely a political aspiration but an operational necessity, requiring sustained investment in European-controlled infrastructure. It highlights Wero and SEPA instant payments as the two pillars of this strategy, noting that all six major French banking groups back EPI.

The timing is pointed. Visa pledged €500 million in European investment in June as the sovereignty debate intensified, and Mastercard has been actively positioning itself within European initiatives such as the ECB's cross-currency TIPS pilot. The FBF paper reads as a response to those moves — an argument that European banks and their governments should not outsource strategic payment capability to non-European schemes, regardless of the investment those schemes offer.

The paper does not break new policy ground, but it crystallises the French banking sector's stance at a moment when EPI faces real tests of adoption. Rabobank's iDEAL-to-Wero migration in the Netherlands and Austrian banking groups joining EPI in recent weeks suggest momentum, but Wero still needs to prove it can compete on merchant acceptance and consumer experience, not just on sovereignty arguments.

*Sources: [Strengthening Europe's sovereignty in payments](https://www.fbf.fr/en/strengthening-europes-sovereignty-in-payments/) — French Banking Federation*
